summary: Defines ACAP, a protocol for storing and accessing program options, configuration and preference data on a remote server. Users can then keep the same settings on different computers.

plainLanguage.summary: ACAP stores application preferences on a server so a user can access them from different network-connected computers. Its datasets support inherited defaults, access permissions and updates that help clients keep local copies in sync.

questions: how to store application preferences on a server
what is the difference between acap and imap
how does acap keep settings synchronized
subtitle: A protocol for remote storage and access of application settings and preferences.

tldr.problem: Application settings can be tied to one computer, making it harder for a user to access the same configuration from another network-connected computer.
tldr.mechanism: The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) stores entries and attributes in hierarchical datasets. It provides commands for searching and updating data, inherited defaults, access controls and quotas.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2244 defines ACAP as a text-based client-server protocol. It is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6075.

today: RFC 2244 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1997. It has been updated by RFC 6075.

sections.title: The Goals of ACAP
sections.content:
The Application Configuration Access Protocol (ACAP) provides remote storage and access for program options, configuration and preferences. Its primary purpose is to let users reach their configuration data from multiple network-connected computers using ACAP-enabled applications.

The design favors simple clients and manageable server data. It includes inheritance for defaults, access control lists for sharing and delegation, and quotas for controlling storage. The server maintains modification times so clients can detect changes, and clients can ask which entries were deleted while they were away.

ACAP is a text-based protocol based on the IMAP framework. It also supports server-side sorting, selective retrieval and change notifications for potentially large datasets or slow connections.
sections.plainLanguage: ACAP keeps application settings on a server so clients can retrieve them from different computers. It also gives clients ways to fetch changes without downloading an entire dataset again.

sections.title: Connections, Commands and Server States
sections.content:
ACAP uses a reliable data stream such as TCP; an ACAP server using TCP listens on port 674. The protocol is text-based and line-oriented, with lines ending in CRLF. Some values are transmitted as literals preceded by their octet count.

Each client command begins with a tag so the client can match server responses to commands. The server can return tagged completion results, tagged intermediate data, untagged updates or a continuation request. A client must be ready to receive any server response at any time, including unrequested updates. Multiple commands may be in progress, subject to flow control.

The server has three states: non-authenticated, authenticated and logout. A successful AUTHENTICATE command moves it into the authenticated state. If a server uses an inactivity auto-logout timer, it must be at least 30 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange tagged commands and responses over a reliable connection. A client must also handle updates that arrive without a specific request.

sections.title: Datasets, Entries and Attributes
sections.content:
An ACAP server exports a hierarchy of datasets. Each dataset contains entries with unique names, and each entry contains named attributes. Attributes can hold one value or a list of values, and metadata describes values and access rights.

Dataset names use a slash-separated hierarchy. Their first component identifies a dataset class; the next component can identify site-wide, group, host or user data. Attribute names use periods between components. Names without a period are reserved for standard attributes, including entry, modtime and subdataset.

ACAP uses relative URLs to refer to subdatasets and to support referrals and inheritance. By default, values may be stored in attributes when the user has the required permission and quota. Server-side validation is required only when the dataset class specification explicitly identifies it.
sections.plainLanguage: A dataset is a named collection of entries, and each entry contains attributes such as settings. The hierarchy shows whether data belongs to a site, group, host or user.

sections.title: Inheritance for Shared Defaults
sections.content:
One dataset can inherit data from a base dataset. The base values appear in the inheriting dataset unless a local STORE changes them. A common arrangement has system-wide or group-wide defaults and a user dataset that adds to or overrides them.

An attribute continues to inherit when it has not been changed locally, or when the client stores DEFAULT for it. Storing DEFAULT restores the inherited value; storing NIL removes the attribute. The server must support at least two levels of inheritance.

Inheritance is named in the dataset.inherit attribute in the dataset's empty-name management entry. A SEARCH with NOINHERIT returns explicit data without inherited values.
sections.plainLanguage: A user dataset can take its starting values from a group or site dataset. A user can change a value locally or restore the inherited default later.

sections.title: Searching, Updating and Monitoring Data
sections.content:
The SEARCH command selects entries, can sort them and can choose which attributes and metadata to return. A client can create a context from matching entries. A context may be enumerated or may request change notifications; it exists only for the session. The server must support at least 100 active contexts in a session.

STORE creates, modifies or deletes entries and attributes. A single STORE command must either apply all its changes or apply none. The UNCHANGEDSINCE modifier can prevent a client from overwriting a newer entry. DELETEDSINCE lists entries removed since a specified time so a client can resynchronize after being disconnected.

Clients can use GETQUOTA to retrieve a dataset's quota limit and usage. The server may send change notifications or quota warnings without being asked for those specific responses.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients can search for matching settings, store changes and ask what was deleted while they were disconnected. A context can report updates during the session so the client can keep its view current.

sections.title: Authentication and Access Control
sections.content:
A connection begins in the non-authenticated state. The AUTHENTICATE command uses a SASL mechanism to identify the user and may negotiate a security layer. ACAP implementations must support CRAM-MD5, although site policy may disable it. A server may also allow anonymous access if it supports the SASL ANONYMOUS mechanism.

Access control lists (ACLs) associate identifiers with rights for a dataset, attribute or attribute value. Standard rights include search, read, write, insert and administer. If an attribute has no ACL, the applicable default ACL for the dataset controls access. A client can use MYRIGHTS to ask which rights it has.

CRAM-MD5 can be attacked with passive password guessing. The RFC notes that hard-to-guess passwords reduce this risk and that ACAP transactions need optional SASL encryption and integrity services or an external security mechanism to protect against observers and modification.
sections.plainLanguage: After authentication, ACLs determine which data a user may search, read, change or administer. Password authentication alone does not encrypt every ACAP transaction, so the connection needs an added security layer to protect data.

sections.title: Protecting Cached Configuration
sections.content:
An ACAP client may cache configuration for use when disconnected. The cache must not be accessible to an unauthorized user. The RFC suggests that a client be able to clear non-public cached configuration when a user leaves a shared computer.

A disconnected-mode client on a laptop may encrypt and password-protect its cached configuration. ACAP URLs have the same security considerations as IMAP URLs.
sections.plainLanguage: Cached settings can remain on a shared or portable computer. The client must prevent unauthorized access and can clear or protect private cached data.
